title: Methods & Data
text:
Data Construction and Measurement


Career, Institution, and City Reconstruction
Person validation, institution normalisation, city standardisation, temporal auditing, and education-employment separation make career histories comparable over time.


Relational Measurement
Coauthorship, mobility ties, publication-location fields, historical platform ties, ego-network measures, and candidate destinations are measured as distinct constructs rather than interchangeable proxies.


Innovation Measurement
Firm-year innovation work links R&D, patents, trademarks, industry, country, identity, and year to compare technological and market-facing innovation without reducing innovation to one count.


Spatial and Temporal Indicators
Remote-sensing and trade-network projects use spatial aggregation, Fisher Information, DTW, K-Means, directed weighted networks, and temporal comparison.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Empirical Design and Modelling


Choice Modelling
Observed moves are organised as event-specific choice sets, with selected destinations compared against alternatives and predictors measured before the move.


Network Analysis
Directed weighted mobility networks, centrality, core structure, ego networks, WERGM, proximity measures, and tie persistence are used to connect macro structures with individual career trajectories.


Comparative and Econometric Designs
The current empirical toolkit includes conditional logit, clustered robust inference, Heckman two-stage models, OLS, robustness checks, sensitivity analysis, and longitudinal comparison.


Method Boundaries
The public profile does not claim deep learning, causal discovery, causal representation learning, survey experimentation, or autonomous LLM research as completed expertise.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Reproducibility and Research Software


Workflow
Research workflows emphasise scripted processing, version control, synthetic fixtures, data-quality audits, source-conflict logs, and separation between public descriptions and restricted data.


Software Environment
Python, R, Stata, ArcGIS/QGIS, NetworkX, Gephi, UCINET, Scimago Graphica, Git, GitHub, and Quarto are used for data construction, modelling, documentation, and publication workflows.


Scopus Research Data Toolkit
The public toolkit supports author-institution-city linkage with synthetic fixtures, offline mock transport, tests, and documentation. It does not bundle licensed Scopus records.
GitHub


Code Availability Boundaries
Public repositories contain reusable workflow code, documentation, tests, synthetic fixtures, and mock transport where sharing is permitted. Reproducible workflows are documented separately from restricted Scopus records, personal-level career data, and licensed source tables. Project-specific code that depends on restricted data can be discussed upon request when data-use conditions allow.

title: Assessment of urban resilience based on nighttime light remote sensing and Fisher’s information method
text:
Authors: Ran Wang · Type: Early research



This early research output evaluates short-term urban resilience during the COVID-19 shock using nighttime-light remote sensing. It combines VIIRS-DNB daily nighttime-light observations with Fisher Information Light and clustering methods to compare city-level changes across major Chinese urban agglomerations. The work connects remote sensing, time-series comparison, and urban resilience assessment, showing how sudden shocks can be observed through changes in urban nighttime activity.




Scientific evaluation of the urban resilience of the city under the impact of the epidemic can provide an important basis for the safe development of the city. Based on the adaptive cycle model, combined with night light day data and Fisher information method, this paper builds Fisher Information Light (FIL), an urban resilience agent index, and uses K-Means clustering based on dynamic time regularization method for 2020 From January 13 to April 8, the urban resilience change patterns of China’s Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei three major urban agglomerations were analyzed and evaluated. The short-term impact and resilience changes of 48 cities, including Beijing and Shanghai, were revealed from the urban agglomeration and urban scale. The results show that:① different urban agglomerations are affected by the epidemic to varying degrees, and the impact of the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration is significantly greater than that of the Pearl River Delta urban agglomeration; different time periods have different impacts on the economic and social life of urban agglomerations. ② In 2019, FIL is on the rise, and the urban system is developing well as a whole. In 2020, FIL has changed dramatically and is in a downward trend. Urban development has been affected to a certain extent. ③Through cluster analysis, urban change patterns are divided into three types: stable cities as a whole show relatively stable fluctuations, the range of change is small, there are troughs in the development stage, rapid recovery, and high sustainable development capabilities. The change curve of low-trough cities is U-shaped and is in a downward trend. Volatuational cities This type of city as a whole shows a steady downward trend.

title: Technology-Brand Innovation Portfolios
text:
Authors: Ran Wang · Status: Research design and data construction in progress



This project examines how patent-based technological assets and trademark-based brand assets co-appear within leading R&D firms. The work treats corporate innovation as a portfolio of different knowledge assets rather than a single count of outputs. At the current stage, the project focuses on indicator construction, portfolio comparison, and descriptive typology based on linked intellectual-property records.




The project develops a measurement framework for comparing technological and brand-oriented innovation portfolios. It links patent and trademark records to firm-year observations and uses that structure to describe how different types of innovation assets are combined. The current stage does not report mature empirical findings; it establishes the data architecture and measurement logic needed for later analysis of firm heterogeneity, industry context, and national innovation environments.

title: Pre-move coauthor ties and the direction of scientific mobility: A city-level choice analysis of highly cited biomedical scientists
text:
Authors: Ran Wang (First author) · Status: Submitted manuscript



This manuscript examines whether direct coauthor ties before a move distinguish the city that a highly cited biomedical scientist actually selects from other candidate cities. It links verified career histories, Scopus coauthorship records, city publication measures, distance, borders, and biomedical specialization within event-specific candidate sets. The design is associational: it compares alternatives within observed moves and interprets coauthor ties as observable bibliometric relations, not as evidence of recruitment, job offers, or causal hiring mechanisms.




Scientific mobility redistributes researchers and knowledge across places. Existing studies document mobility patterns and the roles of personal attributes, city conditions, distance, and national borders. Recent work links professional networks to early-career destinations, but less is known about repeated moves by established scientists or how collaborations differ across candidate cities. This study examines whether highly cited biomedical scientists are more likely to select cities where they already had direct coauthors and whether the number, network share, persistence, and timing of those ties matter. Using verified career histories, Scopus records, and lagged city publication counts, we analyze 336 moves by 217 scientists and 60,024 event-candidate observations drawn from a roster of 500. Event-stratified conditional logit models compare selected cities with alternatives within each move. Cities with at least one direct coauthor in the five years before a move have higher conditional odds of selection than cities without such ties (OR 52.33, 95% CI 35.19-77.81), after controlling for distance, national borders, lagged scientific scale, and biomedical specialization. Among tied cities, more local coauthors and a larger share of the scientist’s observed coauthor network are positively associated with selection. Persistent ties and ties observed in both early and recent periods have stronger associations than nonpersistent or single-period ties. No statistically detectable difference is found between domestic and foreign candidates. The study shows that prior collaboration helps distinguish destination choice beyond city conditions and geographic constraints.

title: Firm-Year Innovation Data System
text:
Authors: Ran Wang · Status: Data system in progress



This project builds a firm-year data system for leading global corporate R&D investors. It connects R&D expenditure, patents, trademarks, industry, country, firm identity, and year so that technology-oriented and market-oriented innovation assets can be analysed in the same empirical structure. The current emphasis is data construction and measurement audit rather than completed causal findings.




The project develops a structured firm-year innovation dataset for high-R&D firms by linking R&D investment, patent records, trademark records, industry classifications, country information, firm identifiers, and time. Its purpose is to support later analysis of corporate innovation portfolios without reducing innovation to a single output count. The current work focuses on entity matching, intellectual-property linkage, panel construction, and measurement consistency.

title: Comparative Study on Biomedical Innovation between China and the United States from the Perspective of Talent Mobility Network
text:
Authors: Ran Wang · Type: Early research



This early research output compares biomedical innovation in China and the United States through the mobility and network positions of top scientists. It uses career histories, publication records, patent information, and innovation-system materials to connect talent mobility with national innovation capacity. The analysis contrasts market-oriented and policy-led innovation environments and uses scientist mobility to interpret differences in research ecosystems, commercialization capacity, and high-end talent accumulation.




Biomedicine has become a major field of technological competition between China and the United States. Drawing on scientific-network theory and the mobility records of top biomedical scientists, this early research output compares the innovation systems of the two countries and discusses the sources of observed differences. The analysis identifies a substantial gap in biomedical innovation capacity. The United States relies on a market-oriented institutional environment, a mature innovation ecosystem, active capital markets, and continued inflows of global scientific talent, forming an innovation model centered on endogenous growth. China has achieved rapid biopharmaceutical growth under policy support, but still faces constraints in core technology accumulation, original innovation capacity, internationalisation, and high-end talent reserves. The Chinese model depends more heavily on government coordination and talent return. While this approach can support resource coordination and strategic mobilisation, market mechanisms, industry-university-research integration, and talent training remain areas for improvement. The study uses talent mobility to interpret differences in biomedical innovation capacity and proposes policy recommendations for strengthening China’s biomedical innovation system.

High-Skilled Mobility · Scientific Collaboration Networks · Corporate Innovation · Urban & Regional Innovation

My research examines how high-skilled researchers move across cities and institutions, and how scientific collaboration and innovation activity are spatially organised around those movements. I build longitudinal relational datasets from career histories, publications, coauthorship records, institutional and city sources, and firm-level innovation data, and use choice models, network analysis, and spatial methods to study mobility, research ties, and regional innovation.





Outside research, I enjoy photography, films, badminton, ultimate frisbee, and swimming.

title: When Coauthorship Goes Quiet: Relational History, Portfolio Context, and the Recurrence of Scientific Ties
text:
Authors: Ran Wang (First author) · Status: Submitted manuscript



This manuscript studies whether prior collaboration history remains associated with later coauthorship recurrence after a complete period of publication dormancy. It follows recurrent dormant coauthor relations among a global highly cited researcher cohort and models annual recurrence risk with discrete-time event-history methods. The interpretation is limited to observable bibliometric recurrence: coauthorship records cannot establish whether researchers stopped communicating, restored trust, or intentionally resumed interpersonal contact.




This study examines the recurrence of scientific coauthorship after publication dormancy. It asks whether deeper prior coauthorship history remains associated with later joint-publication recurrence, and whether that association varies with a focal scientist’s current collaboration-portfolio breadth and elapsed dormancy. The analysis constructs recurrent dormant spells between focal scientists and prior coauthors and estimates discrete-time complementary-log-log event-history models with clustered covariance and standardized adjusted predictions. The results show that deeper pre-dormancy collaboration history is associated with higher recurrence risk. Around average relationship history, broader active collaboration portfolios are also associated with higher recurrence risk, while the history-by-portfolio interaction is negative on the link scale. Standardized predictions indicate that this negative interaction should not be read as a simple decline in absolute probability differences as portfolio breadth increases; dormancy-duration analyses further show that portfolio context is time-dependent.

Around average relationship history, broader active collaboration portfolios are also associated with higher recurrence risk, while the history-by-portfolio interaction is negative on the link scale. Standardized predictions indicate that this negative interaction should not be read as a simple decline in absolute probability differences as portfolio breadth increases; dormancy-duration analyses further show that portfolio context is time-dependent.

title: Analysis on the spatial-temporal evolution of global trade network in the context of the COVID-19
text:
Authors: Ran Wang · Type: Early research



This early research output studies changes in the global commodity trade network during the COVID-19 pandemic. It uses UN Comtrade data from 2019 to 2021 and applies directed weighted network analysis to compare trade structure across countries and product types. The work examines changes in network scale, regional concentration, core countries, and product-specific trade patterns, providing earlier training in global network construction and social network analysis.




Based on the data of the United Nations Commodity Trade Database from 2019 to 2021, this paper uses the social network analysis method to analyze the temporal and spatial pattern evolution of the global trade network under the influence of the COVID-19 epidemic. Research has found that ① There are significant regional differences in trade connections, with North America, Western Europe, and East Asia presenting a “three legged” pattern. ② The United States occupies a core position in the global trade network. The COVID-19 epidemic has reduced the scale of the global trade network and increasingly scattered network connections. ③ China, the United States and Germany are the core countries in the global commodity trade network. The COVID-19 epidemic has different impacts on different types of product trade and countries in different regions. ④ Economy, population, geographical distance, culture, and national policies have varying degrees of impact on global trade.

title: Pre-Move Publication-Location Exposure and Destination Choice among Elite Biomedical Scientists
text:
Authors: Ran Wang · Status: Working paper



This working paper examines whether elite biomedical scientists are more likely to move to candidate cities already present in their pre-move publication-location environment. It organises observed intercity career moves as event-specific destination choices and compares selected cities with alternative destinations. The key measure is place-based exposure: whether a candidate city appeared in the scientist’s origin-anchored publication environment before the move, rather than a verified direct interpersonal tie.

title: Spatial Structure and Determinants of Global Top Biomedical Scientists’ Mobility from an Urban Network Perspective
text:
Authors: Ran Wang (First author) · Status: Accepted · Journal: World Regional Studies



This accepted article examines how the education and employment moves of global top biomedical scientists are organised across cities. Using verified career histories for 500 scientists from 1970 to 2023, it constructs directed intercity mobility networks and relates mobility ties to city-level scientific and institutional conditions. The study distinguishes learning-stage and employment-stage mobility, showing that top-scientist movement is spatially selective, centered strongly on U.S. cities, and patterned differently across career stages.




As a knowledge- and capital-intensive field, biomedicine has become a central arena of global innovation competition. This study focuses on the world’s top biomedical scientists and analyzes their mobility trajectories from an urban-network perspective. Using complex network analysis and Heckman two-stage regression, the paper examines factors associated with scientist mobility across career stages. The study finds that: ① the mobility of top biomedical scientists presents a network structure centered on the United States, with substantial cross-continent movement. In the learning stage, mobility is more unidirectional, concentrated, and unipolar, and top scientists tend to move to university-dense areas. In the working stage, mobility becomes more polycentric and networked, with scientists more likely to choose research institutions and industrial bases. ② Top-scientist mobility is highly selective. Migration is associated with scientific output, academic influence, interdisciplinary background, and related factors. Regions with dense research resources and strong scientific ecology attract top scientists, while institutional barriers and cultural differences constrain global scientific talent mobility.

title: Structure and Formation Mechanisms of Intercity Mobility Networks of Global Top Biomedical Scientists: A Whole-Network and Ego-Network Perspective
text:
Authors: Ran Wang (First author) · Status: Submitted manuscript



This manuscript extends the mobility-network study by combining whole-network and ego-network perspectives. It uses long-term career histories, research-output records, and city attributes for top global biomedical scientists to examine both the structure of intercity mobility ties and the individual positions embedded in those networks. The analysis links network structure, city science conditions, proximity relations, research platforms, and individual career trajectories, treating scientist mobility as a cross-scale spatial process rather than a simple movement count.




Scientific talent mobility is an important force shaping the global innovation landscape. Existing studies, however, have largely explained talent mobility from a whole-network perspective, emphasizing urban science and innovation conditions and multidimensional proximity, while paying insufficient attention to individual career trajectories and the supporting role of research platforms. Using career histories, research outputs, and urban attribute data for top global biomedical scientists from 1970 to 2023, this study combines social network analysis, weighted exponential random graph models, and ego-network analysis to examine the structural characteristics, formation mechanisms, and individual mobility processes of their intercity mobility network. The results show that: (1) The intercity mobility network of top global biomedical scientists exhibits a low-density, highly selective core-periphery structure. Its European and North American core and transatlantic connections remain broadly stable, while cities specializing in medical research, biomedical research and development, and related industrial activities become increasingly prominent in later periods. (2) Intercity mobility ties among top global biomedical scientists are jointly shaped by endogenous network structure, urban science and innovation conditions, and multidimensional proximity. Geographical distance consistently constrains mobility, whereas institutional proximity consistently facilitates it. The effect of cultural proximity weakens in the later period, while cognitive proximity shows no stable association. The effects of urban science and innovation conditions vary across periods and between origins and destinations: specialized research platforms explain mobility more consistently than general economic scale. The initial stock of cross-platform embedded talent is significantly associated with subsequent mobility ties, with a more stable association at the origin. (3) Ego-network analysis shows that the intercity mobility of top global biomedical scientists is a cross-scale spatial process jointly shaped by network structure, urban conditions, multidimensional proximity, historical ties, and individual career trajectories.
